question: Where to hire fractional Chief Revenue Officers?
body:
## Direct Answer

You hire a fractional Chief Revenue Officer through four main channels: specialized fractional-executive networks (Chief Outsiders, Bolster, Go Fractional, Fractionals United), executive-search and staffing firms with a fractional practice, curated marketplaces and talent platforms (Toptal, Continuum, Graphite), and your own warm network of former operators and advisors. The right channel depends on your stage, budget, and how much vetting you want done for you before the first call.

Most B2B companies between roughly $2M and $50M in revenue reach for a fractional CRO when they need senior go-to-market leadership but cannot yet justify a $300K-plus base salary plus equity for a full-time hire. The good news is that the supply of experienced revenue leaders willing to work fractionally has grown sharply, so the harder problem is no longer finding candidates — it is choosing the right sourcing channel and vetting for fit. This guide maps where these leaders actually live, what each channel costs you in time and money, and how to run a hiring process that ends with a revenue leader who moves your pipeline instead of just auditing it.

## What is a fractional CRO and when does hiring one make sense?

A fractional Chief Revenue Officer is a seasoned go-to-market executive who owns your entire revenue engine — sales, marketing alignment, partnerships, and often customer success — on a part-time, ongoing basis, typically one to three days a week under a monthly retainer. Unlike a consultant who delivers a strategy deck and leaves, a fractional CRO carries a number, sits in your leadership meetings, manages your reps, and stays accountable to pipeline and revenue outcomes for the duration of the engagement. They are an embedded operator, not an outside advisor.

The trigger for hiring one is almost always a gap between ambition and leadership capacity. You have product-market fit and a few reps closing deals, but no one is building the repeatable system: the ICP definition, the sales process, the comp plan, the forecasting cadence, the handoffs between marketing and sales. Founders who have been acting as de-facto head of sales hit a ceiling where their time is the bottleneck. A fractional CRO buys you enterprise-grade revenue leadership at roughly 30-50% of a full-time cost, with a faster start and a lower commitment. If you want to pressure-test whether your motion is ready for this kind of leader, our breakdown of [revenue-engine readiness signals](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-cro-readiness) walks through the specific thresholds.

It helps to be precise about what a fractional CRO is *not*, because mislabeled roles are the most common reason an engagement disappoints. A fractional CRO is not a fractional VP of Sales — the VP runs the sales team and the quota, while the CRO owns the entire revenue architecture across sales, marketing, partnerships, and retention, and reports to the CEO or board rather than to another executive. A fractional CRO is not an interim CRO either; an interim leader is a full-time placeholder holding the seat until a permanent hire lands, whereas a fractional leader is a deliberate part-time model you may keep for years. And a fractional CRO is not a growth agency: an agency sells you a service line and its own headcount, while a fractional CRO builds and manages *your* team and hands you an asset you keep after they leave. Getting this taxonomy right before you write the brief saves you from sourcing the wrong archetype through the wrong channel.

There is also a timing question that sits underneath the stage question. The best moment to hire is when you can already see the shape of the problem but do not yet have the bandwidth to solve it — you know your win rate is slipping, or your two best reps are carrying the whole number, or marketing and sales are quietly blaming each other for the pipeline gap. Hiring at that moment gives the fractional CRO a live, diagnosable system to work with. Hiring too early, before you have any repeatable deals, asks a system-builder to do a founder's discovery work; hiring too late, after the wheels have come off a full quarter, forces a turnaround under pressure instead of a build. The sweet spot is the quarter where the problem is visible but not yet on fire.

## Where do fractional CROs actually get hired from?

There are four durable channels, and serious buyers usually run two of them in parallel. **Fractional-executive networks and firms** are the most concentrated supply. Chief Outsiders, Bolster, Go Fractional, Fractionals United, and TechCXO maintain benches of vetted revenue leaders and will shortlist matches to your brief, often within a week. These firms do first-pass vetting for you and frequently guarantee a replacement if the fit fails, which lowers your risk but adds a markup on the retainer.

**Curated talent marketplaces** — Toptal's executive tier, Continuum, Graphite, and Catalant — sit one notch lighter than a full-service firm. They give you a searchable bench and a lighter matching layer, so you keep more control and pay a smaller platform fee, but you do more of the vetting yourself. **Executive-search and staffing firms** with a fractional practice are the option when your revenue is higher and the stakes justify a retained search; they cost the most and move the slowest but go deepest on references and cultural fit. Finally, your **warm network** — former colleagues, investors, advisors, and operator communities like Pavilion or RevGenius — is free, fast on trust, and frequently produces the best single candidate, though it offers no bench depth if the first person says no. The diagram below maps how these channels trade off speed, cost, and vetting.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Need for fractional CRO] --> B{How much vetting do you want done for you}
    B -->|Most vetting| C[Fractional firms and networks]
    B -->|Some vetting| D[Curated marketplaces]
    B -->|Deepest vetting| E[Executive search firms]
    B -->|Trust based| F[Warm network and operator communities]
    C --> G[Shortlist in about one week]
    D --> G
    E --> H[Retained search several weeks]
    F --> I[Single strong referral]
    G --> J[Interview and pilot]
    H --> J
    I --> J
    J --> K[Signed retainer engagement]
```

Each channel has a different center of gravity. If you are early and cost-sensitive, start with your warm network and one marketplace. If you are venture-backed and want speed with a safety net, a fractional firm is the cleanest path. If you are private-equity-owned or preparing for a raise where the revenue leader will be scrutinized, a retained search earns its premium. For a deeper look at how each of these maps to funding stage, see our guide on [matching GTM leadership to company stage](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-gtm-leadership-stage).

There is a fifth, quieter channel worth naming: the operators already orbiting your company. Your investors sit on other boards and see fractional revenue leaders in action across their portfolio, which makes a portfolio-partner referral one of the highest-signal sources you have — the person recommending has watched the candidate actually move a number, not just read a résumé. Your advisors and your own board members frequently either do fractional work themselves or know who is good. And your customers' and partners' former executives — people who already understand your buyer because they sold to or bought from your category — are an underused pool. These sources rarely have a "bench" you can browse, so they do not scale, but a single warm introduction from someone who has seen the candidate deliver often outperforms a dozen cold marketplace profiles. The practical move is to send a crisp one-paragraph brief to five or six trusted operators the same week you engage a firm, then let the two channels race.

A note on where *not* to over-index: generic job boards and open LinkedIn posts will fill your inbox, but they invert the vetting burden entirely onto you and skew toward candidates who are between full-time roles rather than committed career fractional operators. They are not useless — occasionally a strong person surfaces — but treat inbound from a public post as raw ore, not a shortlist, and put every applicant through the same motion-fit screen you would apply to a marketplace profile.

## How much does a fractional CRO cost across these channels?

Pricing is the single biggest source of confusion, because fractional CROs quote in several different structures and the channel you use adds or removes a markup. The most common structure is a **monthly retainer** tied to a committed number of days per week. A one-day-a-week engagement generally runs in the low-to-mid five figures per month; two to three days a week scales up from there. Buying through a full-service firm typically adds a markup over what the same operator would charge you directly, in exchange for vetting, matching, and a replacement guarantee. A marketplace charges a smaller platform fee, and a direct warm-network hire has no intermediary cost at all.

Beyond the retainer, watch for two other structures. Some fractional CROs blend a lower retainer with **performance upside** — a bonus on hitting pipeline or bookings targets, or a small equity grant for longer engagements. Others quote **project or sprint pricing** for a defined scope like rebuilding the sales process or standing up a forecasting cadence, then convert to a retainer if you extend. The important discipline is to price the outcome, not the hours: a leader at a higher day rate who rebuilds your motion in three months is cheaper than a bargain hire who takes a year. Do not fabricate a budget from a competitor's number — get live quotes from three candidates across two channels and compare total cost against the revenue outcome each is underwriting. Our [fractional-executive pricing framework](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-fractional-pricing) breaks down each structure with the questions to ask before you sign.

When you compare quotes, normalize them to a total-cost-of-engagement number rather than a headline day rate, because the sticker figures hide real differences. A firm's retainer bundles the replacement guarantee and the matching work into the price; a direct hire's lower rate may quietly assume you handle the legal paperwork, the onboarding, and the risk of a bad fit yourself. Build a simple comparison that adds the retainer, any performance component at expected attainment, the platform or firm markup, and the implied cost of your own time managing the relationship. Then set that total against the revenue the leader is underwriting. A useful gut check: a fractional CRO who reliably adds even a modest lift to your win rate or shortens your sales cycle by a few weeks generates far more value than their annual cost in most B2B models — the risk is almost never that they are too expensive, it is that they are the wrong fit and you paid for a year of motion that never landed.

Two contract mechanics change your effective cost more than the day rate does. First, the **ramp**: a leader who bills at a lower cadence for the first month while they diagnose, then steps up once the build begins, spreads your risk across the period when you know the least. Second, the **exit terms**: a thirty-day notice provision means your true downside on a bad hire is one month of retainer, not the full engagement, which reframes a seemingly expensive senior operator as a low-risk, cancellable bet. Cheap-looking engagements with long lock-ins and no exit clause are frequently the most expensive mistakes; premium-looking engagements with a clean thirty-day out are often the safest.

## How do you vet and choose the right fractional CRO?

Sourcing is the easy half; vetting is where engagements are won or lost. The failure mode is hiring an impressive résumé whose experience does not match your specific motion. A CRO who scaled an enterprise field-sales org through nine-month sales cycles is often the wrong person for a product-led, self-serve SaaS company, and vice versa. Vet for **motion fit** first: same buyer, same deal size, same sales cycle, same channel. Ask them to walk you through a revenue engine they built from a stage like yours to a stage like your target, with the specific mechanisms — not the outcomes, the mechanisms.

Then run a structured process rather than a series of pleasant conversations. The sequence below is what strong buyers use, and it deliberately front-loads a paid pilot before any long commitment. A two-to-four-week paid diagnostic — where the candidate audits your funnel and returns a prioritized plan — tells you more about how they think and operate than any interview, and it gives them a real look at your data before either side commits to a multi-quarter retainer. Reference calls should target the founders or CEOs they reported to, and the question that matters most is simple: *did revenue actually move, and would you hire them again?*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Shortlist of three to five candidates] --> B[Screen for motion fit]
    B --> C[Working session on your real funnel]
    C --> D[Founder and CEO reference calls]
    D --> E[Paid two to four week pilot diagnostic]
    E --> F{Did they move the right levers}
    F -->|Yes| G[Convert to ongoing retainer]
    F -->|No| H[Part ways and try the next channel]
    G --> I[Set ninety day scorecard]
```

Set a ninety-day scorecard before day one so both sides agree on what winning looks like: pipeline created, sales-process milestones hit, forecast accuracy, and specific hires or systems stood up. Fractional engagements drift when success is undefined, because the leader is only in the building part-time and easy to under-utilize. Clear, written outcomes protect both of you. For a full checklist of vetting questions and red flags, see our [revenue-leader vetting scorecard](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-cro-vetting-scorecard).

Pay attention to the texture of how a candidate talks about past work, because it separates operators from narrators. A genuine operator reaches instinctively for mechanisms and numbers — how the comp plan was structured, why the sales stages were defined the way they were, what the pipeline coverage ratio was, where deals actually stalled — and is comfortable naming what did not work and what they would do differently. A narrator speaks in outcomes and adjectives: "we tripled revenue," "I built a world-class team," "we transformed the go-to-market." Outcomes are easy to borrow; mechanisms are hard to fake. Ask a candidate to whiteboard the exact forecasting cadence they would install in your business in the first thirty days, and you will learn more in fifteen minutes than a résumé tells you in an hour. The working session on your real funnel is the single most predictive step in the sequence — it is the closest thing to watching them do the job before you buy it.

Watch for a short list of red flags. A candidate carrying so many concurrent clients that your one or two days will always lose to a louder engagement is a capacity risk — ask directly how many clients they run and when they last took on a new one. A candidate who resists a paid pilot, or who wants a long lock-in with no exit clause, is signaling that they are optimizing for their own security over your outcome. A candidate whose references are all peers and none are the CEOs or founders they reported to has a gap you want explained. And a candidate who pitches a generic playbook before understanding your specific motion is selling a template, not diagnosing your business. None of these is automatically disqualifying, but each deserves a straight answer before you sign.

## What are the risks of hiring through each channel, and how do you de-risk?

Every channel carries a distinct failure mode. **Firms and networks** can push you toward whoever is on the bench and available now rather than the best possible fit, and the markup means you are paying for matching you might not need. De-risk by insisting on at least three shortlisted candidates and by treating the firm's vetting as a floor, not a ceiling — do your own reference calls regardless. **Marketplaces** put the vetting burden on you, so the risk is a polished profile that hides a thin operating record; de-risk with the paid-pilot step and by verifying the specific revenue claims on real reference calls.

**Retained search** risks over-investing in process for a part-time hire — you can spend six weeks and a large fee to fill a one-day-a-week seat. Reserve it for genuinely high-stakes situations. And the **warm network** carries the subtlest risk: hiring for trust and rapport over motion fit, because a friend's referral feels safe. A great person who has never sold your motion will still struggle. Across all four channels, the universal de-risking tools are the same — a paid diagnostic pilot, founder-level references, a written ninety-day scorecard, and a clean exit clause. Structure the engagement so parting ways at ninety days is cheap and clean, and you convert a high-stakes bet into a series of low-stakes checkpoints. That structure, more than the sourcing channel itself, is what separates fractional hires that transform a revenue org from those that quietly bill for a year and change nothing.

There is one risk that no channel and no contract clause can fully absorb: internal readiness on your side. A fractional CRO cannot succeed against a founder who will not let go of pricing decisions, a data layer so broken that no one can see the pipeline truthfully, or a leadership team that resists the process changes the CRO recommends. Before you sign, make sure the CEO is genuinely ready to grant real authority over the revenue function, that someone owns the CRM well enough for the new leader to trust the numbers, and that the rest of the leadership team is bought into having a part-time operator drive change. The most common quiet failure is not a bad CRO — it is a good CRO who was never given the room to operate. Clearing that internally, before the first day, is the highest-leverage de-risking move available to you, and it costs nothing.

## How do you onboard a fractional CRO so the part-time model actually works?

Because a fractional CRO is only in the building one to three days a week, the first thirty days determine whether the engagement compounds or stalls. The scarce resource is their attention, so the goal of onboarding is to remove every source of friction that would waste it. Give them full access on day one — CRM, dashboards, call recordings, the data room, the comp plans, the last two board decks — so they never spend a billed day waiting on a login. Introduce them to the team explicitly as the owner of the revenue function, with the CEO's authority behind them, so reps and peers do not treat their guidance as optional. Ambiguity about authority is the fastest way to neuter a part-time leader.

The rhythm of the engagement matters as much as the access. Set a fixed weekly cadence — a standing leadership sync, a pipeline review, and a direct line to the CEO — so the relationship does not depend on ad-hoc availability that erodes under everyone's busy weeks. Agree on what happens between their on-site days: who they can delegate to, how decisions get made when they are not in the room, and what gets escalated versus handled. A strong fractional CRO builds a lightweight operating system that runs without them present, which is exactly the asset you are paying for. Map the first ninety days into three phases — diagnose in weeks one to four, build and install in weeks five to eight, and prove the system moves the number in weeks nine to twelve — and hold the ninety-day scorecard as the shared definition of done. Finally, plan for the handoff from the start. The best fractional engagements are designed to make themselves smaller over time: the leader builds the system, hires or elevates the person who will run it day to day, and steps down to a lighter advisory cadence once the machine holds. If you and the candidate both treat the engagement as building something you keep rather than a service you rent, the part-time model stops feeling like a compromise and starts feeling like the most capital-efficient revenue leadership you can buy.

## Related questions

### How is a fractional CRO different from a sales consultant?
A consultant diagnoses and recommends, then leaves. A fractional CRO embeds in your leadership team, owns a revenue number, manages reps, and stays accountable to outcomes for the duration of the engagement.

### How many days a week should a fractional CRO work?
Most engagements run one to three days a week. Early-stage or diagnostic phases often start at one day; active build-out or turnaround phases justify two to three until the system is stable.

### Can a fractional CRO become full-time later?
Frequently, yes. Many fractional engagements are structured as an audition on both sides, and a subset convert to full-time once revenue and funding justify the seat. Agree on the conversion path up front.

### What size company should hire a fractional CRO?
Typically B2B companies between roughly $2M and $50M in revenue that need senior go-to-market leadership but cannot yet justify a full-time executive salary and equity package.

### How long do fractional CRO engagements last?
Most run six to eighteen months — long enough to build a repeatable revenue system and hand it off, but shorter than a permanent hire. Some continue indefinitely at a reduced cadence as an ongoing advisor-operator.

## FAQ

**How quickly can I get a fractional CRO started?**
Through a fractional network or marketplace, you can have a shortlist within a week and a signed engagement in two to three weeks. A warm-network referral can move even faster; a retained search is slower.

**Do fractional CROs work with more than one company at a time?**
Yes. Because they work part-time, most fractional CROs carry two to four clients simultaneously. Ask about their current portfolio to confirm they have real capacity for your engagement and no competitive conflicts.

**Should I hire through a firm or go direct?**
Go through a firm or network when you want vetting, speed, and a replacement guarantee and can accept the markup. Go direct through your network when you already have a strong, motion-matched candidate you trust.

**What should be in a fractional CRO contract?**
A committed cadence in days per week, a monthly retainer, a defined scope, a ninety-day scorecard, IP and confidentiality terms, a non-compete or conflict clause, and a clean thirty-day exit provision for both sides.

**How do I measure whether a fractional CRO is working?**
Track pipeline created, sales-process milestones, forecast accuracy, and specific systems or hires delivered against a scorecard set before day one. Revenue impact lags, so lead with leading indicators in the first quarter.

**Can a fractional CRO hire and manage my sales team?**
Yes — that is often the core of the role. A strong fractional CRO recruits, onboards, coaches, and, when needed, exits reps, and builds the comp plan and enablement they run on. Confirm they have hiring authority in the engagement scope.

**Is a fractional CRO worth it for a pre-revenue startup?**
Usually not. Before product-market fit, you need a founder selling and learning, not a system-builder. A fractional CRO earns their keep once you have early traction and need to make selling repeatable and scalable.

**What industries use fractional CROs most?**
B2B SaaS and technology lead by a wide margin, followed by professional services, manufacturing, healthcare tech, and other complex-sale industries where senior revenue leadership matters but the cost of a full-time CRO is hard to justify early.

**How do I know if I need a fractional CRO or a fractional VP of Sales?**
Choose a CRO when the problem spans the whole revenue engine — marketing-to-sales handoffs, partnerships, retention, and forecasting. Choose a VP of Sales when the team and quota exist and you mainly need someone to run and coach the reps.

**Can a fractional CRO help me raise my next round?**
Indirectly, yes. A fractional CRO who installs clean forecasting, a defensible pipeline, and credible unit economics makes your revenue story far easier to diligence, which is often exactly what investors scrutinize hardest in a growth round.
